title: Tokenization hotpath: async prefetch + shared prefill cache
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: Tokenization and prompt preprocessing on the prefill path contributes disproportionate CPU overhead for short/templated requests. On our short-response workloads tokenization accounts for ~15-25% of end-to-end p95 latency and creates CPU hotspots on ingress workers. Goal: reduce prefill-side tokenization overhead and 95th percentile latency impact while keeping memory and multi-tenant safety bounded.

Proposed approach: 1) Async token-prefetch: start lightweight tokenization work at request ingress as an async job that races with auth/route checks so tokenization can complete earlier without blocking request orchestration. 2) Shared LRU prefill cache: global in-process cache on serving nodes keyed by deterministic fingerprint (org_id, model_name, model_hash, tokenizer_config_hash, prompt_prefix_hash). Cache stores token ids + kv-cache-ready metadata to avoid repeated tokenization for common templated prompts. 3) Fast-paths: a) ASCII/whitespace-only quick-scan that maps to a byte-tokenization fast path using a lightweight table lookup; b) micro-batch tokenization for concurrent identical prompts to amortize overhead; c) fall back to full tokenizer when needed. 4) Memory & safety: per-node and per-org quotas, size-based eviction + TTL (default 5m) to bound memory; optional encrypted keys and scrubbed cache values to avoid leaking sensitive PB. 5) Backpressure & concurrency controls: limit concurrent prefetch tasks per-worker and global tokenization thread pool. 6) Observability: emit tokenization_time_ns, tokenization_cpu_ns, cache_hit_ratio, cache_size_bytes, avg_tokens_cached.

Engineering trade-offs and rationale: - Async prefetch lowers tail latency for short responses but introduces additional concurrency complexity and potential CPU spikes. We'll mitigate with rate-limiting and a tokenization thread pool. - Shared cache yields high hit-rates for templated prompts (expected 40-70%) but increases memory footprint; we enforce per-org quotas and eviction. - Fast-path scanner drastically reduces CPU for ASCII-only prompts with negligible quality difference; however need careful correctness testing for language edge-cases.

Implementation plan (high level): Phase 1: prototype async prefetch + metrics and microbench harness. Phase 2: implement shared LRU cache with pluggable key strategy and TTL, add per-org scoping. Phase 3: add ASCII fast-path and micro-batching coalescing. Phase 4: safety hardening, tests, and 1% canary rollout behind feature flag.

Benchmarks / targets: - Reduce median tokenization time for short prompts by >=60% and p95 by >=50%. - Achieve cache hit >= 50% on templated workload sample. - Keep per-node memory delta < 8GB for worst-case 1000 active orgs via quotas.
acceptance_criteria: Instrument tokenization_time_ns and cache_hit_ratio and publish dashboard
Async prefetch enabled behind feature flag with thread-pool and backpressure
Shared cache implemented with per-org scoping, size/TTL eviction, and integration tests
ASCII fast-path reduces CPU on targeted workload by >=60% in synthetic and sampled traces
End-to-end p95 latency improvement >=10% for short-response route on canary traffic
Canary rollout plan and rollback documented and exercised

Current staging sample results: cache_hit_ratio 62% on templated set, average cached token length 42, memory delta ~+220MB per 1k active orgs at default TTL (need per-org quota tuning).
notes: Rollout plan: feature flag -> 1% canary -> 10% -> 50% -> 100% with automated rollback on tokenization_time_ns p95 regression or cache_memory_bytes > threshold

Alternative considered: offloading tokenization to a separate autoscaled service. Rejected for now due to cross-service latency and complexity; keep option open for later if memory costs unacceptable.
QA: need fuzz tests for unusual unicode sequences and end-to-end decode equivalence checks.
